endorsements.quote: Prompt engineering or other in-context learning should be performed using a development dataset that is also kept separate from the final test dataset.
Along with datasets used and code used for analysis, all prompts tested should be released, along with corresponding results.

Drawing from best practices set out for all model development, the checklist also includes a section to report clinical model cards14 or labels15 that summarize the model capabilities, intended use, train ing data and limitations, potential biases, and model risks (Fig. 2 ).
Generative model performance should be compared with rigorously selected baseline models, which may include other generative models but also non-generative approaches.
Analysis of model performance across diverse patient subgroups and data subtypes to identify biases is strongly encouraged.
These models should also be scrutinized for up-to-date cybersecurity vulnerabilities, such as adversarial prompt injections2, and other potential model harms.
The source of the labels, including annotation guidelines and inter-annotator agreement for human labels, should be clearly documented.

unlisted_practices: Report training data, fine-tuning data, and retrieval sources, and guard against training data memorization, leakage, and contamination.
Split data at the patient level so all data from each patient appear in only one split.
Report data, code, prompts, model versions, hyperparameters, random seeds, and compute requirements in secure repositories using tiered transparency levels.
Release model weights to secure repositories with appropriate use agreements and treat them with the same care as clinical datasets.
Conduct blinded human expert evaluation of generative model outputs and report evaluator guidelines, experience, and inter-reviewer variability.
Do not use model-generated explanations as a method of explainability; rigorously evaluate explainability methods when applied to new clinical tasks.
Perform error analysis and prompt sensitivity and ablation tests to understand how generative models fail.
Distinguish overlap accuracy, semantic accuracy, and clinical utility metrics and justify primary metrics; do not rely on BLEU or ROUGE alone for clinical accuracy.
Engage diverse clinical evaluators to assess cultural and social biases and perform external validation for fairness and robustness.
Report cohort selection criteria reproducibly using standard ontologies and describe deviations of datasets from real-world settings.

screen.reason: The title describes a reporting checklist (MI-CLAIM-GEN) for generative AI in health, which is a guideline/framework.
